title: Acharya Balkrishna Says Turmeric Milk Is Ayurveda’s Go-To Cold and Cough Remedy
excerpt: The Patanjali chairman’s prescription for cold season: warm milk, turmeric and a pinch of black pepper — supportive care backed by real pharmacology, but not a cure.
body:
• Acharya Balkrishna, the Ayurveda expert and chairman of Patanjali Ayurved, calls turmeric Ayurveda’s go-to remedy for cold and cough, delivered as warm turmeric milk (haldi doodh).
  • The key compound is curcumin — described in The Statesman as “a bioactive compound famous for its strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects.”
  • His preparation: one cup of warm milk with half to one teaspoon of turmeric and a pinch of black pepper to boost curcumin absorption; drink before bedtime, with honey, cinnamon or ginger optional.
  • Medical fact-checks urge caution: “turmeric cures cough in 5 minutes” claims are misleading — turmeric is supportive, not a cure.

As flu season approaches, one of India’s best-known Ayurveda voices is making the case for a kitchen-staple remedy. Acharya Balkrishna — Ayurveda expert, author and chairman of Patanjali Ayurved — says turmeric is Ayurveda’s go-to remedy for cold and cough, and his prescription is the classic haldi doodh: warm milk with a teaspoon of turmeric.

Balkrishna’s explanation, laid out in The Statesman’s health series, centers on curcumin, turmeric’s signature bioactive compound, “famous for its strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects.” According to Balkrishna, a cup of warm turmeric milk “calms the throat, decreases inflammation, and loosens phlegm, making it an essential drink during flu season.” He also says it “relieves respiratory problems such as asthma and congestion and acts as an infection guard,” with the anti-inflammatory content helping to open airways, thin mucus and relieve breathing trouble.

“Consuming warm milk with a teaspoon of turmeric is of great benefit. It relieves respiratory problems such as asthma and congestion and acts as an infection guard.”

— Acharya Balkrishna, via The Statesman

The recipe

The preparation is simple. Balkrishna’s version: one cup of warm milk — dairy or plant-based — with half to one teaspoon of turmeric powder and a pinch of black pepper. The pepper matters: piperine, black pepper’s active compound, substantially increases the body’s absorption of curcumin (one widely cited figure puts the boost at more than 2000%). Honey, cinnamon or ginger can be added for taste and warmth. The recommendation is to drink it before bedtime.

Balkrishna has been pressing the same message on his social channels. “अत्यंत लाभकारी है #हल्दी का #दूध” — “Turmeric milk is extremely beneficial” — he wrote on X in 2024, and the turmeric-milk explainer remains the anchor of his cold-season guidance.

Supportive, not a cure

The Ayurvedic case for turmeric rests on real pharmacology — curcumin’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties are well documented in published research. But medical fact-checkers draw a line at the stronger claims. MedicalDialogues’ fact-check found “turmeric cures cough in 5 minutes” style claims misleading: turmeric can support respiratory comfort, but it is not a cure, and a persistent or severe cough still needs proper medical evaluation.

Balkrishna’s remedy explainers in The Statesman reach a broad Indian audience — he was honoured with the “I AM PEACEKEEPER – Champion Health Award 2026” for his Ayurveda advocacy. For the diaspora audience stocking up for winter, haldi doodh is a low-cost comfort measure backed by a plausible mechanism — with the usual caveat that a home remedy is no substitute for a doctor when symptoms persist.
